title: Vital Signs
subtitle: Data Visualization II · pivot, heatmap, facet & read the plot
story: You're an Alaskan hospital's instrument technician, clocking off at last — one step from the elevator, and one step from finally meeting the person you've been hoping to go out to dinner with for months. They're up in the break room waiting for you. Then the pharmacist catches your sleeve. “Before you go — I need a hand. A patient, Elias, came in fading this morning, and I can't make sense of his data on my laptop. Can you have a look?”

done.title: Right treatment, in time
done.body: Creatinine ran highest in Elias's panel, so it's renal strain — and Elias gets Nephrocidin. Great job!

rooms.title: The pharmacy
rooms.debrief: First you reshaped the data — pivot_wider, one column per metabolite — so two variables could be plotted against each other: choline versus 2-aminoisobutyric acid, with a fit line. Looking at how two variables relate is a key data analysis technique.
rooms.technique: pivot_wider + geom_point/geom_smooth — correlate two metabolites (proxy marker)

rooms.designNote: METABOLOMICS REWRITE (2026-07-30). TECHNIQUE unchanged — pivot_wider (long→wide) + geom_point + geom_smooth (two continuous). STORY: 2-aminoisobutyric acid is a slow/expensive assay; is choline a trustworthy proxy? TASK: pivot metabolomics_hospital wider (one col per metabolite), plot 2-AIB vs Choline + geom_smooth. VERIFIED (20 patients): tight positive, Pearson r = 0.99 pooled (and holds within group: healthy 0.95, kidney 0.98 — deliberately NOT a Simpson pair; room 3 is). ≥6 options; correct = strong positive (idx 3). Sets up room 3's Simpson twist on a DIFFERENT pair.

question.prompt: The pharmacist says: “Elias's panel is missing a marker I need — 2-aminoisobutyric acid — and that assay is slow and expensive. Choline is quick and cheap, and I'm hoping it correlates with 2-aminoisobutyric acid tightly enough to stand in for it. I've got the analysis started, but can't figure out the plotting. Please can you plot 2-aminoisobutyric acid against choline for all 20 patients, with a straight line through them? What does it tell you — is choline a trustworthy stand-in?”
options: No relationship — the points scatter with no trend, so choline tells you nothing about 2-aminoisobutyric acid.
A negative relationship — patients high in choline run low in 2-aminoisobutyric acid, so choline would mislead you.
A weak positive trend — the points loosely rise but scatter widely, so choline is only a rough guide.
A strong positive line — 2-aminoisobutyric acid rises clearly with choline.
A curved relationship — choline predicts 2-aminoisobutyric acid at high values but flattens out at low ones.
A curved relationship — choline predicts 2-aminoisobutyric acid at low values but flattens out at high ones.

feedback.correct: Correct — logged: 2-aminoisobutyric acid tracks choline almost perfectly, so choline is a safe stand-in.
wrong: Look at the overall shape of the cloud: do the points rise together, fall, or just scatter? Add the smoothing line and see how tightly they hug it.
The points sit almost exactly on one rising line — that's a very strong positive link. Check that it holds across the whole range, not just at one end.
Even setting the most extreme patient aside, the rest still rise tightly together — so the relationship is real, not an artefact of one outlier.

rooms.designNote: METABOLOMICS REWRITE (2026-07-30). TECHNIQUE — geom_tile HEATMAP (2 discrete × 1 continuous). STORY: Elias's chemistry is barely characterised — find the prior patient most like him as a reference. TASK: bind Elias (metabolomics_hospital_unknown) to the cohort, EXCLUDE Creatinine (the renal assay is still pending — this both hides the boss answer and gives a clean match), scale() each metabolite, geom_tile(metabolite × patient, fill = level). VERIFIED ANSWER: Patient 54 (Elias ≈ patient 54; nearest d = 0.10 vs 2nd 1.00, margin 0.89). Elias is engineered as patient 54's near-twin + a Creatinine spike, so 54 is his clean single match. ≥6 patient options (54,58,56,57,52,60); correct = Patient 54 (idx 1). No boss leak: Creatinine is not in this panel.

entry.title: Going up
entry.text: Choline tracks 2-aminoisobutyric acid almost perfectly, so you tell the pharmacist yes — choline is a safe stand-in for the marker she needs. The elevator doors close. Your phone buzzes: another delay! Elias is fading fast and they need you in the lab to help read more data. A colleague has texted over the ward's patient survey — 20 prior patients, some healthy and some with kidney-disease, fully profiled. Elias's chemistry is barely characterised — start by finding the patient most like him, so you have a reference point for understanding his results.

hotspots.label: The phone in the wall clip
hotspots.starterCode:
metabolomics_hospital %>%
mutate(patient_number = as.character(patient_number)) %>%
bind_rows(dplyr::mutate(metabolomics_hospital_unknown, patient_status = "Elias")) %>%
filter(metabolite != "Creatinine") %>%
group_by(metabolite) %>%
mutate(level = as.numeric(scale(concentration))) %>%
ungroup() -> metabolomics_hospital

metabolomics_hospital

question.prompt: The data analysis is started, but not finished. Draw a heatmap — metabolite and patient on the axes, colour intensity from each metabolite's scaled level — and find the patient whose whole row of tiles looks most like Elias's. (Creatinine, the specialist renal assay, is still pending from the lab, so it's not in the panel yet.) Which patient is Elias' closest chemical match?
options: Patient 58
Patient 54
Patient 56
Patient 57
Patient 52
Patient 60

feedback.correct: Correct — logged: patient 54 is Elias's closest chemical match, so it's the case to reason from.
wrong: Find Elias's row of tiles first, then scan the other rows for the one whose colours match it most closely across every metabolite.
Scaling matters — without scale(), one high-concentration metabolite drowns out the rest. Once every column is on the same footing, one patient's row mirrors Elias's far better than the others.
Plenty of patients are 'quiet' (every tile mid-range) and so resemble each other; the match you want mirrors Elias's pattern across the whole row, highs and lows alike.

rooms.title: The corridor
rooms.debrief: The trap, and a lesson. Pooled together, indoxyl sulfate and p-cresyl sulfate tracked almost perfectly — until you faceted by patient status and the single clean line broke apart. Splitting a plot by group can overturn what the whole looked like. We should always ask whether one trend is really something else in disguise.
rooms.technique: pivot_wider + geom_smooth + facet_wrap(~patient_status) — does the correlation differ by group?

rooms.designNote: METABOLOMICS REWRITE (2026-07-30). TECHNIQUE — pivot_wider + geom_point + geom_smooth + facet_wrap(~ patient_status) (small multiples). STORY: a colleague challenges the assumption that indoxyl sulfate and p-cresyl sulfate (two gut toxins) are linked. TASK: pivot wide, plot p-cresyl vs indoxyl, facet by patient_status. VERIFIED: SIMPSON'S PARADOX — pooled r = 0.95, but within healthy r = -0.22 and within kidney r = 0.21; the tight pooled line is an artefact of the two groups sitting at different levels. (This pair is ENGINEERED into the dataset to carry the Simpson effect — see sample_data note.) ≥6 options; correct = the 'vanishes within group' conclusion (idx 4).

entry.title: The corridor
entry.text: Patient 54 is Elias's chemical twin — nearly identical across every metabolite — so at least you have a comparison to work from. You are three doors from the lab when a colleague catches your arm: “The pharmacist told me that you helped them with a correlation problem. I have one too: indoxyl sulfate and p-cresyl sulfate, two gut-derived toxins, seem nicely correlated, but we have doubts that they are equally correlated once healthy patients and ones with kidney-disease are separated. Can you please check that before you go in?”

question.prompt: Plot p-cresyl sulfate against indoxyl sulfate, then facet by patient_status (healthy vs kidney_disease). Pooled together the line looks almost perfect (r ≈ 0.95). Once you split it by group, what's the right conclusion?
options: The link is just as tight inside each group — faceting confirms the two toxins always rise together.
The correlation is strong in healthy patients but disappears in the kidney-disease group.
The correlation is strong in the kidney-disease group but disappears in healthy patients.
Both groups show a strong negative relationship once separated.
Within either group the relationship all but vanishes — the tight pooled line is largely an artefact of the two groups sitting at different levels, not a real within-patient link.
The groups can't be compared because each holds a different number of patients.

feedback.correct: Correct — logged: split by group, the indoxyl–p-cresyl link all but vanishes; the pooled line only looked tight because the two groups sit at different levels.
wrong: Look at each group's panel on its own: within the healthy points alone, and within the kidney points alone, do they still sit on a tight line — or scatter?
The pooled line is steep and clean, but each group's own cloud is nearly shapeless. What does that tell you about where the pooled correlation really comes from?
This is Simpson's paradox: two groups at different levels can fake a strong overall trend that isn't there within either one.

rooms.designNote: METABOLOMICS REWRITE (2026-07-30). ASSESSED BOSS. STORY: Elias's renal assay is finally back; his condition is one of five syndromes, each flagged by one metabolite running high (creatinine→renal strain→Nephrocidin; methylmalonate→B12 block→Cobalatide; hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid→tyrosine overload→Tyrostat; 1-methyladenosine→nucleoside surge→Adenoquel; myoinositol→osmolyte imbalance→Inositex). TASK: bind Elias to the cohort, find which of the five he is most abnormally high on (markers are on different scales — must compare each to the cohort, e.g. z-score). VERIFIED: Creatinine is Elias's clear outlier — z = +6.0 vs healthy / +3.6 vs full cohort (next marker −4.4z away) AND the dataset max → Nephrocidin. OPTIONS: the five treatments + Glucostat decoy; correct = Nephrocidin (idx 0). ASSESSMENT NOTE: this REPLACES the former alaska_lake_data exercise (exercises.csv '[exercises] data visualization ii' Q1) — exercises.csv is now DECOUPLED and may need a matching metabolomics entry if this boss is still the graded item.

entry.title: The lab
entry.text: Your colleague is right — pool the groups together and the indoxyl–p-cresyl line looks perfect, but split it by patient group and it falls apart. Worth remembering. The lab doors part. Elias is stable but fading — and the renal assay is finally back, so his panel is complete at last. His condition seems likely to be one of five syndromes, each flagged by a different metabolite running high. Compare his panel to the patient cohort, find the marker he's most abnormal on, and you'll know what to treat.

question.prompt: Elias's renal assay is back, so his panel is complete. His condition is one of five syndromes, each flagged by one metabolite running high: renal strain (creatinine → treat with Nephrocidin), B12 block (methylmalonate → treat with Cobalatide), tyrosine overload (hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid → Tyrostat), nucleoside surge (1-methyladenosine → Adenoquel), osmolyte imbalance (myoinositol → Inositex). Compare Elias's panel to the patient cohort, find which of those five metabolites he runs most abnormally high on — and so which treatment he needs.
options: Nephrocidin
Cobalatide
Tyrostat
Adenoquel
Inositex
Glucostat

feedback.correct: Correct — logged: creatinine runs far higher in Elias than in any patient in the cohort, so it's renal strain and Elias gets Nephrocidin.
wrong: The five metabolites are on wildly different scales, so you can't just compare Elias's raw numbers to each other. Compare each of his markers to the cohort — how many standard deviations above the patients' average does each sit? — and find the one where he's the extreme outlier.
Only five metabolites are in play, each keyed to a syndrome. Among just those five, Elias is off the chart on exactly one of them.
Some of Elias's markers sit near the middle of the pack; one sits far above every other patient. That single extreme marker is the one that names his syndrome — and his treatment.

rooms.title: The break room
rooms.debrief: The escape was the chapter's signature technique done by hand — no console at all. You arranged nine postcards into a 3×3, season down the page and remoteness across, and read the answer straight off the middle row. That is faceting: split the pile by the right two variables and the pattern you need lines up where you can read it.
rooms.technique: facet by hand — arrange the nine postcards into a 3×3 grid (season × remoteness) and read the middle row

entry.title: One more thing
entry.text: The break room at last — and there's the person you've been waiting to see, looking up from a table buried in postcards. “You made it! I'm nearly done — I'm laying out readers' summer postcards for the tourism magazine. I started the arrangement on the back of the door. Once you help me finish, we can go for dinner!” Postcards everywhere, an editor's note on the table, and a keypad by the door.

rooms.designNote: BREAK ROOM — v3 facet-collage escape (WIRED 2026-07-21). Ungraded, out of the codec. Postcards are opaque pickup clues → the notebook collage board (boardCols 3); the started-collage clue is the non-pickup format key; the way-out door is gated on the keypad and fires escapeDone. hotspots.label: Editor's note
hotspots.body:
A note from the magazine editor:

“Love the postcard collage idea! For the spread, take the reader through the season — run them from the first of summer at the top down to the tail end of summer at the bottom. Then, take them left to right by how far you've got to go to get there: the easy roadside stops on the left, the deep backcountry on the right. I don't care how long anyone stayed — that's not the story. It's when, and how far out. The issue runs early next week!”

escape.enterLabel: The collage on the door still isn't finished…

escapeDone.title: Dinner, at last
escapeDone.body: Season down the page, roadside to backcountry across — the three postcards along the middle read off the code, and the keypad blinks green. Your crush sweeps the pile into a folder, grabs their coat, and smiles and you head out the door. Elias is stable, and the magazine spread is complete. Now go enjoy dinner.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: One dataset, read four different ways — pivoted, plotted, heat-mapped, and faceted — until the numbers named a diagnosis and saved a life. Here is how each room taught a different way of looking at data, and how the escape was the same skill.
